---
title: "Behaviour: How synthetic respondents answer"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5,
                      dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
```

Two sets of answers can land in the same score deciles and
still be given in very different ways. Behaviour compares how synthetic and
real respondents answer, with eight features per respondent. This tutorial
covers `behaviour_features()`, `flag_careless()`, `synthetic_behaviour()`
and `gg_behaviour()`.

These functions take the raw answers and an item table, and do the keying
themselves.

```{r}
library(synthcheck)

h <- hexaco_items[hexaco_items$trait == "H", ]
real <- hexaco_real[hexaco_real$country == "Canada", ]
ca <- hexaco_llm[hexaco_llm$country == "Canada" & hexaco_llm$attempt <= 3, ]
```

## The eight features

| Feature | What it measures | Careless side |
|---|---|---|
| `variability` | SD of the raw answers | Very low or very high |
| `extreme` | Share of answers at the lowest or highest category | High |
| `midpoint` | Share of answers at the middle category | High |
| `acquiescence` | Mean raw answer minus the scale midpoint | High |
| `key_inconsistency` | Gap between positive and reverse-keyed items of a facet | High |
| `even_odd` | Agreement of odd and even items across facets | Low |
| `mahalanobis` | Distance of the facet means from real people | High |
| `person_fit` | $l_z$ under a graded response model fitted to the real data | Low; very high means "too coherent" |

`behaviour_features()` gives the eight values for every respondent. The
reference for Mahalanobis distance and person fit comes from the real data:

```{r}
syn1 <- ca[ca$attempt == 1, ]
f_syn <- behaviour_features(syn1, h, real = real)
f_real <- behaviour_features(real, h)

rbind(real = sapply(f_real, median, na.rm = TRUE),
      synthetic = sapply(f_syn, median, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Person fit fits one graded response model per scale with mirt, on the real
data only. It is the slowest feature. `fit_scales = character(0)` skips it,
which is handy while you explore.

## Careless real respondents

Real data have careless respondents too. `flag_careless()` flags a real
respondent when at least two of the eight features fall in the most extreme
2.5% on the careless side:

```{r}
fl <- flag_careless(real, h)
mean(fl$careless)
table(fl$n_flags)
```

By default synthcheck compares synthetic respondents with all real
respondents, because that is the data people can actually collect.
`clean_real = TRUE` in `synthetic_behaviour()` and `authenticity_benchmark()`
compares them with the real respondents left after the flagged ones are
removed. `careless_rule` takes your own rule: A function of the feature table
that returns `TRUE` for careless respondents.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
strict <- function(f) f$variability < 0.5 | f$person_fit < -3
flag_careless(real, h, rule = strict)
```

## The Behaviour index

`synthetic_behaviour()` cuts the real values of each feature at their deciles
and counts the share of synthetic respondents in each decile, as Overlap does
for score deciles. A feature scores 100 when synthetic respondents spread over
the real deciles like real people, and 10 when they all fall in one decile.
Behaviour is the mean over the eight features.

```{r}
beh <- synthetic_behaviour(as_synthetic_list(ca), real, h)
beh
```

```{r, fig.height = 5}
gg_behaviour(beh)
```

Each cell is one feature for one model. The number is $B_f$, red means the
synthetic median is lower than the real one, blue means higher, and the
shade shows how far the feature is from real people. Here the common pattern
is "too tidy": Key inconsistency and acquiescence are lower than in real
people (red), while even-odd consistency and person fit are higher (blue).
Synthetic respondents answer more consistently than real people do.

`by = "attempt"` draws one row per attempt to show how stable each model is:

```{r, fig.height = 7}
gg_behaviour(beh, by = "attempt")
```

The summary also gives the person fit tails: The share of synthetic
respondents below the real 5th percentile of $l_z$ (careless-like) and above
the real 95th percentile (too coherent). Real data have 5% in each.

```{r}
beh$summary[, c("model", "lz_low", "lz_high")]
```

No model has careless-like respondents. The medians of person fit are higher
than in real people, but few synthetic respondents pass the real 95th
percentile: They fit the model a little better than typical real people, not
better than the most coherent ones.
